[Monte Carlo integration](monte-carlo-integration.qmd) used draws from the normalized posterior grid. **Importance sampling** instead draws from a proposal distribution and corrects its mismatch with the unnormalized passage-level Student-t posterior through weights.

## Reweighting a proposal

For target density $f$, proposal density $g$, and integrand $h$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}_f[h(\eta)]
&=
\int h(\eta)\frac{f(\eta)}{g(\eta)}g(\eta)\,\mathrm d\eta\\
&=
\mathbb{E}_g[h(\eta)w(\eta)],
\end{aligned}
$$

where $w(\eta)=f(\eta)/g(\eta)$. If the target is known only as $\widetilde f(\eta)=Zf(\eta)$, normalized weights

$$
\widetilde w^{(s)}
=
\frac{\widetilde f(\eta^{(s)})/g(\eta^{(s)})}
{\sum_{r=1}^S\widetilde f(\eta^{(r)})/g(\eta^{(r)})}
$$

remove the shared unknown constant. The self-normalized estimator is

$$
\widehat I_S
=
\sum_{s=1}^S\widetilde w^{(s)}h(\eta^{(s)}).
$$

It is generally biased at finite $S$, but consistent under the required support and integrability conditions.

## Assessing importance weights

The code reconstructs the same posterior grid used on the preceding page. It then draws 30,000 values from a bivariate $t_5$ proposal centered at the grid mean with scale $1.5\widehat\Sigma$. The proposal is calibrated to this computation target, not interpreted as a linguistic distribution.

```{r}
#| label: provo-importance-sampling
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv("data/provo/passage-summaries.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
y <- provo$noun_minus_verb_log_ffd
nu <- 4
prior_scale <- 2 * sd(y)

log_sum_exp <- function(x) {
  maximum <- max(x)
  maximum + log(sum(exp(x - maximum)))
}
log_posterior_eta <- function(eta) {
  mu <- eta[1]; sigma <- exp(eta[2])
  sum(dt((y - mu) / sigma, df = nu, log = TRUE) - log(sigma)) +
    dnorm(mu, 0, prior_scale, log = TRUE) +
    log(2) + dnorm(sigma, 0, prior_scale, log = TRUE) + eta[2]
}
mode_fit <- optim(c(median(y), log(mad(y))),
                  function(eta) -log_posterior_eta(eta),
                  method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE,
                  control = list(reltol = 1e-12, maxit = 1000L))
local_sd <- sqrt(diag(solve(mode_fit$hessian)))
grid <- expand.grid(
  mu = seq(mode_fit$par[1] - 7 * local_sd[1],
           mode_fit$par[1] + 7 * local_sd[1], length.out = 321L),
  log_sigma = seq(mode_fit$par[2] - 7 * local_sd[2],
                  mode_fit$par[2] + 7 * local_sd[2], length.out = 321L)
)
grid$log_kernel <- apply(grid, 1, log_posterior_eta)
grid$weight <- exp(grid$log_kernel - log_sum_exp(grid$log_kernel))
grid_mean <- colSums(grid[, c("mu", "log_sigma")] * grid$weight)
centered <- sweep(as.matrix(grid[, c("mu", "log_sigma")]),
                  2, grid_mean, "-")
grid_covariance <- crossprod(centered * sqrt(grid$weight))

rmvt <- function(n, location, scale, df) {
  dimension <- length(location)
  normal <- matrix(rnorm(n * dimension), nrow = n)
  standard <- sqrt(rchisq(n, df = df) / df)
  sweep(normal %*% chol(scale), 1, standard, "/") +
    matrix(location, nrow = n, ncol = dimension, byrow = TRUE)
}
dmvt_log <- function(x, location, scale, df) {
  dimension <- length(location)
  centered <- sweep(x, 2, location, "-")
  inverse <- solve(scale)
  quadratic <- rowSums((centered %*% inverse) * centered)
  log_determinant <- determinant(scale, logarithm = TRUE)$modulus[1]
  lgamma((df + dimension) / 2) - lgamma(df / 2) -
    .5 * (dimension * log(df * pi) + log_determinant) -
    .5 * (df + dimension) * log1p(quadratic / df)
}

set.seed(2026101803)
S <- 30000L
proposal_df <- 5
proposal_scale <- 1.5 * grid_covariance
eta <- rmvt(S, grid_mean, proposal_scale, proposal_df)
log_weight <- apply(eta, 1, log_posterior_eta) -
  dmvt_log(eta, grid_mean, proposal_scale, proposal_df)
weight <- exp(log_weight - log_sum_exp(log_weight))

importance_ess <- 1 / sum(weight^2)
summary <- data.frame(
  mean_mu = sum(weight * eta[, 1]),
  probability_mu_positive = sum(weight * (eta[, 1] > 0)),
  mean_exp_mu = sum(weight * exp(eta[, 1])),
  raw_weight_ess = importance_ess,
  largest_weight = max(weight),
  top_100_weight_share = sum(sort(weight, decreasing = TRUE)[1:100])
)
stopifnot(length(y) == 55L, abs(sum(weight) - 1) < 1e-12)
summary
```

The raw-weight effective sample size,

$$
\operatorname{ESS}_w
=
\frac{1}{\sum_{s=1}^S(\widetilde w^{(s)})^2},
$$

is `r format(round(importance_ess), big.mark = ",")` from 30,000 proposal draws. It summarizes weight concentration, not Markov-chain dependence and not the number of Provo passages.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-importance-weights
#| fig-cap: "Proposal draws for the passage-level Student-t model. The accent marks the one percent with the largest normalized weights."
proposal_draws <- data.frame(
  mu = eta[, 1], sigma = exp(eta[, 2]), weight = weight
)
weight_cutoff <- quantile(weight, .99)

proposal_opacity <- .16
weighted_opacity <- .65
ggplot(proposal_draws, aes(mu, sigma)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey70", alpha = proposal_opacity, size = .55) +
  geom_point(data = subset(proposal_draws, weight >= weight_cutoff),
             color = "#8B1A1A", alpha = weighted_opacity, size = .8) +
  labs(x = "Passage-level contrast (mu)",
       y = "Passage contrast scale (sigma)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The proposal must cover every target region of positive probability. Shared support is not sufficient for efficiency: if $q$ places little mass in an important target region, a few weights dominate. The largest weight and the mass in the largest 100 weights diagnose that realized concentration but cannot prove that an unseen tail was covered.

The proposal distribution is a computational device. Its unweighted draw frequency is neither a prior nor a statement about passage contrasts. Only the weighted empirical distribution approximates the passage-level Student-t model.

## Check your understanding

1. Why does self-normalization remove the target normalizer?
2. What fails when $g(\eta)=0$ in a target region?
3. Why can full support still yield poor efficiency?
4. What does $\operatorname{ESS}_w$ count in this calculation?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Every raw weight contains the same unknown multiplicative target constant, which cancels when weights are divided by their sum. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The weight ratio is undefined there, and proposal draws can never represent that positive-probability part of the target. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. A proposal may have full support but place very little mass in an important target region, causing a few extreme weights to dominate. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. $\operatorname{ESS}_w$ is the number of equally weighted proposal draws with roughly comparable weight information; it is not a passage count or a Markov-chain ESS. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
